svg.title: How a stop request is taken, stored, and enforced on every later submission
svg.desc: Two paths that meet at one table. On the left, someone asks not to be contacted. The opt-out route deliberately has no Turnstile and no identity check: under TCPA a revocation must be honoured through any reasonable means, and friction on a stop request is itself the risk. The request is validated, the email is lowercased and the phone is reduced to its last ten digits, and the row is written with a hashed address. That reduction is the one canonical form, shared with the validation schemas, because storage and lookup once had separate versions of it and a number written differently stayed contactable. On the right, a later contact form submission is captured. Before anything is queued, the suppression check matches the submitted email or the submitted digits against that table. A match does not discard the submission: the person did fill in the form, so the lead is still stored as a record. What a match stops is the outbox row, so nothing is delivered to the CRM or the dialer, and it stops the acknowledgement email. The visitor still receives a success response, because telling them they are suppressed would leak that someone else's record exists. Releasing a suppressed lead is a human decision. A suppression row carries no retention date, because it has to outlive the lead it suppresses.
